newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani ex-minister moves house by camel.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani ex-minister moves house by camel.

text.p: A minister in Benazir Bhutto's ousted government vacated his official residence in unusual style on Wednesday, using a camel caravan to move his household goods from the Pakistani capital of Islamabad to Lahore.

Julius Salik, former population and welfare minister, ceremonially burned his suits, offered his blood to commemorate people who died before Pakistan's creation in 1947, and mounted a camel cart for the 320-km (200-mile) journey to his home town.
Salik, a member of Pakistan's minority Christian community, has a history of staging bizarre public spectacles.
Caretaker prime minister Meraj Khalid gave Salik special permission to bring camels into the orderly boulevards of Islamabad, from which pack animals are banned.
The national anthem played as the seven camels carried 300 portraits of Nobel prize winners collected by Salik, who has been nominated by Bhutto for the 1997 Nobel peace prize.
Salik had a nurse draw blood from his arm and then poured it on the ground in tribute to the hundreds of thousands of people who died in the run-up to independence in 1947.
He offered the most original explanation to date for the fall of Bhutto's government, sacked by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.

"I have played the national anthem before leaving the official residence to correct a mistake...made on Pakistan's independence day on August 14 when the flag-hoisting ceremony was cancelled because of rain," he said.
"I believe our government was dismissed because we failed to hoist the flag on our national day and the former prime minister cut the national flag on the cake."

Salik, who usually wears the traditional shalwar kameez (long shirt and trousers), set fire to his five suits outside his former residence in the ministers' enclave to show his disapproval of lavish state spending by debt-ridden Pakistan.
"This is the only way you can bury the VIP culture," he said as he distributed cloth bought with money he had raised to provide destitute women with clothing on their wedding day.

Salik's camel train will cost at least 10 times as much as it would cost to move his goods by truck. The camel cart owners will be paid 1,000 rupees ($25) a day besides their meals throughout the seven-day trip to Lahore.
